modules.name: prelude
modules.summary: Functions that need no import
modules.description: These names are always available. `String`, `str`, `List<T>` and the `Display` trait need no import either. Types, `null`, `?` optionals and error unions are part of the language itself: see the guide.

params.doc: a format string, or any single value

functions.name: panic

params.name: template

functions.doc: Ends the program immediately. Destructors do not run.

modules.summary: string -> number conversion with real error handling.
modules.description: Both functions accept an optional sign and decimal digits only. Whitespace, `1e3` and `0x10` are rejected with `InvalidDigit`.

modules.name: fmt
modules.summary: how values turn into text.
modules.description:
`Display` is the trait behind `println(x)`, `to_str(x)` and `"{x}"` for your own types: implement it and
the value prints the way you wrote. It is part of the prelude, so no import is needed.

Types without an impl can still be shown with `{value:?}`, the automatic representation:
`Point { x: 1, y: 2 }`.

traits.name: Display
traits.doc: The trait behind `println(x)`, `to_str(x)`, `x.to_string()` and `"{x}"`. Implement it for your own types and they print the way you wrote. It is part of the prelude, so no import is needed. All built-in number types and `bool` implement it already, so `T: Display` bounds accept them.

methods.name: to_string
methods.doc: Builds the text for this value. A format such as `{p:>10}` applies to the text this returns.

modules.name: math
modules.summary: constants, libm bindings and small integer helpers.
modules.description: `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `atan2`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `floor`, `ceil` and `fabs` are the libm functions of the same name (all `f64`). The `_i32`, `_i64` and `_f64` helpers exist because plain `min`/`max` live in `std.mem` and are generic.
modules.example:
import std.math;

println("{:.4}", math.sqrt(2.0));        // 1.4142
println("{}", math.gcd(48, 18));          // 6
println("{}", math.max_i32(3, 9));        // 9
println("{:.5}", math.PI);                // 3.14159

consts.doc: the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter

modules.name: list
modules.summary: a growable array that works for every element type.
modules.description:
A List owns its elements: it is destroyed automatically at the end of its scope, running each
element's destructor (and freeing `String` elements). Elements with destructors can only be moved
in and out (`push`, `pop`, `remove`) or borrowed (`at`); copying accessors such as `get` and
`extend` need a copyable element type.

errors.doc: `pop` was called on an empty list

errors.name: NotFound
errors.doc: `find_by` found no matching element

modules.name: tree
modules.summary: an ordered set kept in a binary search tree, for every element type that implements `Ord`.
modules.description:
Numbers, `str` and `String` are ordered already. For your own types, implement `Ord`:

The tree owns its elements (an equal element is not inserted twice) and is destroyed automatically
at the end of its scope. Inserting, finding and removing take time proportional to the tree's height.
`has`, `get` and `remove` take the value to look for by value (a `String` probe is consumed).

modules.name: own
modules.summary: std.own (EXPERIMENTAL): memory with an owner. No collector, no borrow checker, and no manual free().
modules.description:
An `Own<T>` is the single owner of one heap value. It is moved like a `String` (`let b = a;` leaves `a` unusable), and when the
owner goes out of scope the value is destroyed and its memory is freed on the spot, so allocation costs what `malloc` costs and
nothing ever pauses. What `Own` does NOT do is stop you from keeping a pointer past that point. Instead of proving it away
(borrowing rules) it makes it detectable: every block carries a generation number that changes when the block is freed, and a
`Ref<T>` remembers the number it was made with. `r.get()` compares them and panics with "use of a freed value" if they differ,
so a dangling `Ref` is a clean panic, never silent corruption. `Own.at()` is the fast, unchecked borrow for code that
already holds the owner. When ownership really is shared, `Rc<T>` counts its owners and frees the value when the last one goes.

Limits: `Rc` counts are not atomic (do not share an `Rc` between threads), `Rc` cycles leak, freed blocks are recycled but never
returned to the system, and a raw `*T` taken from `at()` is as unchecked as any pointer.

A Socket closes itself at the end of its scope (or with `close()`). Calls that wait for the network are
collector safepoints, so other threads keep running and collecting while one is blocked.

modules.name: http
modules.summary: a small HTTP/1.1 client over std.net (plain `http://` only; there is no TLS).
modules.description:
`headers` is text with one `Name: value` per line. Every request sends `Connection: close`, so the
answer is complete when the server closes the connection. Responses with `Content-Length` and
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked` bodies are understood. Failures: BadUrl, Unsupported (an `https://` URL),
BadResponse, and the std.net errors (ResolveFailed, ConnectFailed, Timeout, ...).

modules.name: thread
modules.summary: OS threads, mutexes, condition variables, channels (pthread through FFI).
modules.description:
Threads share the garbage-collected heap. The collector parks every thread at its next allocation or
blocking call; Mutex.lock, Condvar.wait, Thread.join and thread.sleep_ms tell it that they are blocking.
A thread that computes for a long time without allocating only delays collections, it never breaks them.

modules.name: async
modules.summary: `async fn` and `await`, built on OS threads (std.thread).
modules.description:
Calling an async function returns a task (a pointer to a Task, TryTask, Job or TryJob, below). `await task`
is the same as `task.wait()`: it blocks the calling thread until the task is done and gives back its
value (or its error). Await every task exactly once: the result is moved out, and an awaited thread is
the one that gets cleaned up. Tasks share the garbage-collected heap, so pass them data, not stack
pointers. Async functions cannot be generic and cannot take `self`.
